cards.lessonTitle: What a backend actually is
cards.prompt: A shopping app checks in the browser that a coupon is valid and lowers the price shown. Where must the price be enforced for the discount to be safe?
options: In the browser, since it already checks
On the server, when the order is placed
In the database column type only
cards.explain: A client can be modified or bypassed entirely. Only the server, which the owner controls, can be trusted to enforce prices and discounts.

cards.lessonTitle: What a backend actually is
cards.prompt: The counter server above has handled 5 requests. You restart the process and call it once. What does it return?
cards.explain: The counter lives in the process's memory. A restart creates a new process with visits at 0, so the next response is 1.

cards.lessonTitle: What a backend actually is
cards.prompt: You run two identical copies of the counter server behind a load balancer. A user calls it four times and sees the numbers 1, 1, 2, 2. What is the cause?
options: Each copy keeps its own in-memory counter, so state is not shared
HTTP is stateless so counters cannot work
cards.explain: Each process has a private variable. Alternating requests hit different copies, so each counts its own. Shared state must live in a store both copies use.

cards.lessonTitle: What a backend actually is
cards.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
options: The backend is your program plus the runtime and system beneath it; a framework is one library inside it
A backend is always a database
A backend must be written in Node.js
cards.explain: Frameworks help with parsing and routing. The backend is the whole running system that holds state, applies rules and answers requests.

cards.lessonTitle: Anatomy of a request
cards.prompt: Which stages can be skipped on a second request when the connection is reused?
options: DNS lookup, TCP handshake and TLS handshake
cards.explain: Name resolution and the TCP and TLS handshakes belong to the connection. Reuse them and only the per-request stages remain.

cards.lessonTitle: Anatomy of a request
cards.prompt: The server is very far away; a single network round trip takes 100 ms. A brand new HTTPS connection (TCP then TLS 1.3) is opened and the request sent. Roughly how long before the server begins to process the request, ignoring DNS?
cards.explain: TCP takes one round trip (100 ms), TLS 1.3 one more (100 ms), then the request needs half a round trip to arrive (50 ms): about 250 ms before your code even starts.

cards.lessonTitle: Anatomy of a request
cards.prompt: Users in another continent report that your API feels slow. Your handler takes 4 ms. What should you check first?
options: Rewrite the handler in a faster language
The timing breakdown: DNS, connect, TLS and time to first byte for those users
cards.explain: With a 4 ms handler, the time is almost certainly in distance and connection setup. Measure the stages before changing code.

cards.lessonTitle: Anatomy of a request
cards.prompt: One endpoint loads a list of 50 posts, then runs a separate database query for each author. It is slow even though each query takes 1 ms. Which description explains it?
options: Fifty sequential round trips to the database add up; the work should be batched
cards.explain: Each query pays a round trip plus execution. Fifty of them in sequence cost far more than one query that fetches all authors together.

cards.lessonTitle: Names, addresses and ports
cards.prompt: A server listens on one IP address and one port. How can it hold thousands of simultaneous TCP connections to different clients?
options: Each connection gets its own server port
Connections are distinguished by the full four-tuple, so many clients can share the same server IP and port
It cannot; it must fork one process per port
UDP is used for the extra connections
cards.explain: A TCP connection is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port. Clients differ in source IP or source port, so the same server endpoint serves them all.

cards.lessonTitle: Names, addresses and ports
cards.prompt: A record has TTL 300. At t=0 a resolver fetches it. At t=100 you change the record at the authoritative server. A client asks that resolver at t=200. What does it get?
options: The old address, because the cached copy is still within its TTL
An error until the cache is flushed
cards.explain: The resolver is allowed to serve its cached copy until t=300. Changes propagate only as old cached entries expire.

cards.lessonTitle: Names, addresses and ports
cards.prompt: Your Node service makes thousands of short outbound requests per second and you see sporadic latency spikes that also slow down file reads. What is the most plausible cause to investigate first?
options: dns.lookup calls queueing in the libuv thread pool
cards.explain: dns.lookup uses getaddrinfo on the shared thread pool (default 4 threads). Slow lookups can occupy every thread and delay unrelated pool work such as fs operations.

cards.lessonTitle: Names, addresses and ports
cards.prompt: Two different websites resolve to the same IP address. How does the server know which one a request is for?
options: The hostname is carried in the request (the Host header, or SNI during TLS)
Each site uses a different TCP port automatically
It cannot; this setup is impossible
cards.explain: Name-based virtual hosting: the client states which hostname it wants inside the request, so one IP can serve many sites.

cards.lessonTitle: TCP and the cost of a connection
cards.prompt: The round-trip time to a server is 100 ms. You open a fresh TCP connection and send one small request. Roughly how long before the server can start processing the request (ignoring TLS)?
options: About 100 ms for the handshake, then the request travels the remaining one-way trip
cards.explain: The handshake takes one full RTT (SYN out, SYN-ACK back). The client then sends its request, which needs another half RTT to arrive. Roughly 1.5 RTT in total before processing begins.

cards.lessonTitle: TCP and the cost of a connection
cards.prompt: A line-based chat server does `socket.on('data', c => handle(c.toString()))` and treats each chunk as one message. It works locally but sometimes merges or splits messages in production. What is the root cause?
options: TCP is a byte stream and does not preserve write boundaries, so the server must buffer and split on a delimiter
Node.js has a bug in net
The client needs to send messages more slowly
cards.explain: Chunk boundaries are arbitrary. Accumulate bytes in a buffer and extract complete messages by delimiter or length prefix.

cards.lessonTitle: TCP and the cost of a connection
cards.prompt: Which property does TCP itself provide?
options: Reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream
cards.explain: TCP gives reliability and ordering. Encryption and authentication come from TLS, and latency is bounded below by the speed of light plus handshakes.

cards.lessonTitle: TCP and the cost of a connection
cards.prompt: Your service calls an internal API 500 times per second, each time with a brand new connection, and p99 latency is high even though the API is fast. What is the best first change?
options: Add more CPU to the API
Reuse connections with keep-alive or a pool
Lower the TTL on the DNS record
cards.explain: Each new connection pays at least one round trip for the handshake (more with TLS). Reusing connections removes that cost from almost every request.

cards.lessonTitle: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, identity
cards.prompt: Which set correctly names what TLS provides?
options: Confidentiality, integrity, authenticity of the server
cards.explain: TLS keeps data secret, detects tampering and lets the client verify the server's identity. It does not provide anonymity.

cards.lessonTitle: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, identity
cards.prompt: An observer on your Wi-Fi watches your HTTPS request to https://shop.example.com/orders/42?coupon=SAVE. Which part can they typically NOT see?
cards.explain: Path, query, headers and body are inside the encrypted channel. IP address and SNI hostname are visible in the clear in the usual setup.

cards.lessonTitle: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, identity
cards.prompt: To fix 'unable to verify the first certificate' in staging, a teammate sets rejectUnauthorized: false in production code. What did they actually break?
options: Nothing, the data is still encrypted so it is equally safe
Identity verification: the client will now accept any certificate, so a man-in-the-middle can read and alter traffic
Only the performance of the handshake
cards.explain: The channel is still encrypted, but to whoever answered, including an attacker. Fix the chain or trust store instead of disabling verification.

cards.lessonTitle: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, identity
cards.prompt: A mobile app and your Node backend fail with a certificate error on your new API host, but desktop browsers load it fine. What is the likeliest cause?
options: The server is not sending the intermediate certificate, and browsers are silently fetching it
TLS 1.3 is not supported by the phone
The DNS TTL is too long
cards.explain: Browsers may fetch missing intermediates, but many HTTP clients and backends will not. Configure the server to send the full chain.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, threads and waiting for I/O
cards.prompt: What do two threads of the same process share?
cards.explain: Threads share the process's memory (heap), which is why sharing is easy and races are possible. Each thread has its own stack and registers.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, threads and waiting for I/O
cards.prompt: A blocking thread-per-request server has 10,000 idle connections each waiting on a slow upstream. What is the main resource being wasted?
options: CPU cycles, because the waiting threads spin
Memory and scheduling overhead for parked threads
cards.explain: Parked threads do not use CPU, but each holds stack memory and adds scheduler bookkeeping. That is what limits connection count.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, threads and waiting for I/O
cards.prompt: In the readFile example, which prints first: the text 'both started', or the file lengths?
options: It depends on the file size only
cards.explain: readFile returns a promise immediately. The synchronous console.log runs before the awaited results arrive.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, threads and waiting for I/O
cards.prompt: A Node endpoint computes a 2-second loop of pure arithmetic per request. During it other requests stall. What is the cause and the right fix?
options: The database is slow; add an index
The loop occupies the only JavaScript thread; move it to a worker thread or another service
Node cannot handle HTTP; switch protocols
The OS is out of memory
cards.explain: Pure computing never yields to the event loop, so nothing else runs on that thread. Offload CPU-heavy work to workers or other processes.

cards.lessonTitle: The Node.js event loop, step by step
cards.prompt: In the order.cjs program, which line prints third?
cards.explain: Both sync lines print first. Then nextTick callbacks run before promise microtasks, so 3 nextTick prints third.

cards.lessonTitle: The Node.js event loop, step by step
cards.prompt: async function f(){ await null; console.log('A'); } f(); setTimeout(()=>console.log('B'),0); console.log('C'); What is the output order?
cards.explain: C is synchronous. The continuation after await is a microtask and runs before the timer. So C, A, B.

cards.lessonTitle: The Node.js event loop, step by step
cards.prompt: A function recursively schedules itself with Promise.resolve().then(self). Your server stops answering HTTP requests, yet no function shows heavy CPU work in a profile. Why?
options: The microtask queue never empties, so the loop never reaches poll
cards.explain: Microtasks drain fully before the loop continues. A self-rescheduling microtask means the queue is never empty, so I/O callbacks never run.

cards.lessonTitle: The Node.js event loop, step by step
cards.prompt: Inside a fs.readFile callback you schedule both setTimeout(fn,0) and setImmediate(fn2). Which runs first?
cards.explain: After the poll phase the loop goes straight to check, where immediates run. The timers phase comes on the next turn, so the immediate wins deterministically.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, signals and exit codes
cards.prompt: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored by a program?
cards.explain: SIGKILL is handled by the kernel directly, so the process gets no chance to clean up.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, signals and exit codes
cards.prompt: A process is stopped by SIGTERM (signal 15). What exit status does a shell usually report?
cards.explain: Shells report 128 plus the signal number: 128 + 15 = 143.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, signals and exit codes
cards.prompt: A CI step 'npm run build | tee build.log' passes even though the build crashed. Why?
options: The pipeline's exit status is the last command's (tee), unless pipefail is set
cards.explain: Without pipefail only the final command's status counts. Use set -o pipefail.

cards.lessonTitle: Processes, signals and exit codes
cards.prompt: Your container starts the app with a shell wrapper and 'docker stop' always takes 10 seconds before killing it. What is the likely cause?
options: SIGTERM goes to the shell, not the app, so the app never shuts down gracefully until the SIGKILL timeout
cards.explain: Signals go to PID 1. If that is a shell that does not forward them, use exec so the app receives SIGTERM.

cards.lessonTitle: Files, permissions and a reproducible dev environment
cards.prompt: Which mode makes a private key readable and writable only by its owner?
cards.explain: 600 means read and write for the owner and no access for group or others.

cards.lessonTitle: Files, permissions and a reproducible dev environment
cards.prompt: Starting your server fails with 'address already in use'. What is the first diagnostic command?
options: ss -ltnp to see which process is listening on the port
cards.explain: ss shows the listening socket and, with -p, the owning process, so you can see whether it is a stale copy of your own server.

cards.lessonTitle: Files, permissions and a reproducible dev environment
cards.prompt: A path traversal bug lets an attacker read arbitrary files, and your app runs as root. Why is this worse?
options: As root the attacker can read or overwrite any file on the machine, not just the app's
cards.explain: A process's authority is its user's authority. Running unprivileged limits what an exploit can reach.

cards.lessonTitle: Files, permissions and a reproducible dev environment
cards.prompt: What most directly makes 'works on my machine' bugs less likely?
options: Pinned runtime versions and a committed lockfile
cards.explain: Identical language and dependency versions across machines remove a major source of differences.

cards.lessonTitle: HTTP as text on a socket
cards.prompt: Which line correctly ends the header section of an HTTP/1.1 message?
options: A line containing only a semicolon
A blank line (CRLF CRLF after the last header)
cards.explain: A completely empty line separates headers from the body. Everything after it is body.

cards.lessonTitle: HTTP as text on a socket
cards.prompt: A server sends the body 'héllo' encoded as UTF-8 and sets Content-Length: 5. What does a client observe?
options: A truncated body, because the UTF-8 byte length is 6
The body padded with a null byte
cards.explain: Content-Length counts bytes. 'é' takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the body is 6 bytes, and the client stops reading after 5.

cards.lessonTitle: HTTP as text on a socket
cards.prompt: You run three identical API servers behind a load balancer and a user's second request lands on a different server than the first. Which design makes this work without special routing?
options: Store the user's session in server memory
Each request carries what is needed to identify the user (token or session id looked up in shared storage)
Pin each user to one server forever
cards.explain: Stateless requests can be served by any replica. Continuity must come from data the client resends, backed by shared state if needed.

cards.lessonTitle: HTTP as text on a socket
cards.prompt: Your raw parser only handles requests that arrive in a single data event, and a large POST sometimes fails. What is the bug?
options: The request can arrive in several chunks, so the parser must buffer until headers and the declared body length are complete
Node closes sockets on large payloads
cards.explain: TCP delivers a byte stream. You must accumulate bytes, find the end of headers, then read exactly Content-Length body bytes.

cards.lessonTitle: Methods, status codes and the headers that matter
cards.prompt: A client times out after sending DELETE /orders/9 and wants to retry safely. Why is that allowed?
options: DELETE is idempotent: repeating it leaves the same final state
Retries are always safe in HTTP
cards.explain: Idempotency is about the resulting state. Deleting an already deleted order leaves it deleted, although the response may differ.

cards.lessonTitle: Methods, status codes and the headers that matter
cards.prompt: A logged-in user requests an admin page they are not allowed to see. Which status best describes this?
cards.explain: The server knows who they are (authenticated) and refuses (not authorised), which is 403. 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid.

cards.lessonTitle: Methods, status codes and the headers that matter
cards.prompt: A client sends If-None-Match: v17 and the server’s current ETag is v18. What happens?
options: 200 with the full body and the new ETag
cards.explain: The condition (my copy is current) is false, so the server sends the full new representation along with its new ETag.

cards.lessonTitle: Methods, status codes and the headers that matter
cards.prompt: Users complain that items vanish from their cart overnight. Logs show a search crawler requesting /cart/remove?item=3 links. What is the design error?
options: A state-changing action is exposed as GET, which is assumed safe and gets prefetched or crawled
The cart uses too many headers
cards.explain: GET must be safe. Use POST, PUT or DELETE for state changes so crawlers, prefetchers and caches never trigger them.

cards.lessonTitle: CORS: why browsers police cross-origin calls
cards.prompt: Which URL is the SAME origin as https://shop.example.com/cart?
cards.explain: Origin is scheme + host + port. Only the path differs in https://shop.example.com/checkout.

cards.lessonTitle: CORS: why browsers police cross-origin calls
cards.prompt: A teammate says: 'We do not need auth on this endpoint because CORS only allows our frontend.' What is the flaw?
options: CORS is enforced by browsers only, so curl or any server-side script can call the API freely
cards.explain: Non-browser clients do not enforce CORS. It protects users of browsers, not your API.

cards.lessonTitle: CORS: why browsers police cross-origin calls
cards.prompt: A page at https://app.example.com sends fetch with method PUT and header Content-Type: application/json to https://api.example.com. What does the browser do first?
options: Sends an OPTIONS preflight asking whether the method and headers are allowed
Blocks the call without contacting the server
cards.explain: PUT and a JSON content type make this a non-simple request, so the browser preflights with OPTIONS before sending the real request.

cards.lessonTitle: CORS: why browsers police cross-origin calls
cards.prompt: Your API sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and credentialed fetches from the browser fail. Why?
options: Wildcard origins are forbidden when credentials are included; the server must echo a specific allowed origin
Cookies cannot be used over HTTPS
cards.explain: Browsers reject the combination of * and credentials. Return the exact requesting origin from an allowlist and add Vary: Origin.

cards.lessonTitle: Routes are a lookup table
cards.prompt: Pattern /users/:id/posts/:postId. Which request path gives postId equal to the text 7?
cards.explain: Segments must line up: users, a value for id, posts, a value for postId. Only the first path has that shape.

cards.lessonTitle: Routes are a lookup table
cards.prompt: Routes exist for GET /users/:id and DELETE /users/:id. A client sends POST /users/42. What is the correct response?
options: 405 Method Not Allowed with Allow: GET, DELETE
cards.explain: The path matches, only the method is unsupported. 405 plus an Allow header tells the client exactly what is possible.

cards.lessonTitle: Routes are a lookup table
cards.prompt: A handler does fs.readFile('./files/' + params.name). Requesting /files/..%2F..%2Fsecret returns a private file. What went wrong?
options: The router matched the wrong pattern
The decoded parameter contained ../ and was joined into a path without validation
cards.explain: Percent-decoding turns %2F into a slash. The parameter is untrusted input and must be validated, not concatenated into a file path.

cards.lessonTitle: Routes are a lookup table
cards.prompt: Your metrics dashboard has a separate line for every user id because it records the raw URL. What should it record instead?
options: The matched route pattern such as /users/:id
cards.explain: The pattern groups all ids into one series, keeping label cardinality small while still saying which endpoint was hit.

cards.lessonTitle: Order, specificity and edge cases
cards.prompt: Express routes registered in this order: GET /users/:id, then GET /users/me. What does GET /users/me return?
options: The /users/:id handler with id equal to me
cards.explain: First match wins. The parameterised route is first and matches the text me, so the specific route is never reached.

cards.lessonTitle: Order, specificity and edge cases
cards.prompt: Your /health route never runs; every request to it returns 404 JSON from app.get('*'). What is wrong?
cards.explain: The catch-all matches everything and stops the search. Specific routes must be registered before it.

cards.lessonTitle: Order, specificity and edge cases
cards.prompt: Both /products/9 and /products/9/ return 200 with identical content. Why might that hurt, and what is a fix?
options: Caches and search engines treat them as two pages; redirect one form to the other with a 301
It is faster, so keep it
cards.explain: Two URLs for one resource split caches and analytics, and complicate access rules. Choose a canonical form and redirect the rest.

cards.lessonTitle: Order, specificity and edge cases
cards.prompt: By default, what does Express return for POST on a path that only has a GET route?
cards.explain: Express does not synthesize 405 for you. Add it deliberately if you want clients to get an Allow header.

cards.lessonTitle: Text, bytes and JSON
cards.prompt: In Node, const s = 'héllo 👋'. Which gives the number of bytes in UTF-8?
cards.explain: length counts UTF-16 code units and the spread counts characters. Buffer.byteLength counts UTF-8 bytes, which is what Content-Length needs.

cards.lessonTitle: Text, bytes and JSON
cards.prompt: Your database ids are 64-bit integers like 9007199254740993. A browser client shows the wrong record. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The id was sent as a JSON number and rounded to a float; send ids as strings
cards.explain: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floats and cannot represent every integer above 2^53 exactly. Strings preserve the digits.

cards.lessonTitle: Text, bytes and JSON
cards.prompt: What does JSON.stringify({a: undefined, b: NaN, c: null}) produce?
cards.explain: undefined properties are omitted, NaN becomes null, and null stays null.

cards.lessonTitle: Text, bytes and JSON
cards.prompt: An API returns a total of 0.30000000000000004 for 0.10 + 0.20 rupees. What is the right design?
options: Use integer minor units (paise) in the API and format for display
Send it as a float with more digits
cards.explain: Binary floats cannot represent most decimals exactly. Integers in the smallest unit avoid the error entirely.

cards.lessonTitle: Binary formats, schemas and compatibility
cards.prompt: How many bytes does the varint encoding of the number 300 take?
cards.explain: 300 needs 9 bits. Seven bits fit in the first byte, so it needs a second byte: ac 02.

cards.lessonTitle: Binary formats, schemas and compatibility
cards.prompt: Bytes 08 96 01 12 03 61 64 61 under the schema (id = 1 varint, name = 2 string). What is name?
cards.explain: Tag 12 is field 2, length-delimited, length 3, and the three bytes 61 64 61 are 'ada' in UTF-8.

cards.lessonTitle: Binary formats, schemas and compatibility
cards.prompt: You retire a field numbered 4 and later add a new field also numbered 4 with a different type. Old clients are still deployed. What happens?
options: Nothing, numbers are free to reuse
Old clients write data the server reads as the new field, causing silent corruption; reserve retired numbers instead
The compiler always rejects it at runtime
cards.explain: The wire identifies fields by number. Reuse changes the meaning of bytes already in flight, and nothing signals an error.

cards.lessonTitle: Binary formats, schemas and compatibility
cards.prompt: Which situation most justifies a binary format over JSON?
options: A public API used by browsers and curl
High-volume internal calls between two services you control
A small config file edited by hand
cards.explain: Internal, high-volume, schema-controlled traffic gains most from smaller messages and faster parsing, while the lost readability costs least.

cards.lessonTitle: Passwords and server-side sessions
cards.prompt: A user is logged in and requests another person's invoice. Which concept decides whether this is allowed?
cards.explain: Authentication established who the user is. Authorization decides what that identity may access.

cards.lessonTitle: Passwords and server-side sessions
cards.prompt: Why is a deliberately slow hash used for passwords?
options: To make each guess expensive for someone who steals the hashes
Because fast hashes are not one-way
cards.explain: A legitimate login hashes once, an attacker must hash billions of guesses. Slowness multiplies their cost without hurting normal users much.

cards.lessonTitle: Passwords and server-side sessions
cards.prompt: A site sets the cookie uid=7 after login and trusts it. What is the flaw?
options: A client can edit the cookie to uid=8 and act as another user
uid must be hashed with MD5
cards.explain: Anything the client holds can be altered. The cookie must be an unguessable random session id that maps to a user only on the server.

cards.lessonTitle: Passwords and server-side sessions
cards.prompt: A user reports their laptop was stolen while logged in. With server-side sessions, how do you cut off access immediately?
options: Wait for the cookie to expire
Delete that user's session records in the store
Change the cookie name in the code
cards.explain: The server is the source of truth. Deleting the session records makes the stolen cookie useless on the very next request.

cards.lessonTitle: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization
cards.prompt: What does a standard JWT's signature guarantee?
options: The payload was not modified since it was signed
The user is still logged in
cards.explain: A signature gives integrity and authenticity, not secrecy. Anyone can read the payload, and the token stays valid until its expiry.

cards.lessonTitle: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization
cards.prompt: You issue 24-hour JWTs. An employee leaves and you want access cut now. What is the problem, and a common mitigation?
options: JWTs cannot be verified; use cookies
No server record exists to delete; use short-lived access tokens with a revocable refresh token
The signature must be re-signed daily; use bigger keys
HTTP caches the token; clear the cache
cards.explain: Stateless tokens stay valid until expiry. Short access lifetimes plus a revocable refresh token limit the window.

cards.lessonTitle: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization
cards.prompt: GET /invoices/42 returns any invoice to any logged-in user who knows the id. What is missing?
options: An ownership check comparing the invoice owner with the authenticated user
cards.explain: Authentication was done, authorization was not. The handler must verify that this user may access this invoice.

cards.lessonTitle: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization
cards.prompt: For a single traditional web app with one database and a need to log users out instantly, which choice is usually simplest?
cards.explain: With a single app and a store available, sessions give instant revocation without extra mechanisms.

cards.lessonTitle: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization
cards.prompt: A server reads the algorithm from the incoming token header and a forged token says alg is none with no signature. If the server accepts it, what happens?
options: Rejected, since the signature is missing
The forged claims are trusted, so anyone can impersonate any user
cards.explain: Letting the attacker choose the verification method lets them choose no verification. Always fix the accepted algorithm in server configuration.

cards.lessonTitle: Never trust input: validate at the edge
cards.prompt: Your signup form validates the email in JavaScript before submitting. Why must the server validate it again?
options: Requests can be sent without the form, so only server-side checks protect the server
cards.explain: The server cannot know that the request came from your form. Anyone can send the same HTTP request with a script, skipping every client-side check.

cards.lessonTitle: Never trust input: validate at the edge
cards.prompt: With the parseCreateUser function above, what does parseCreateUser({ email: 'A@x.io', age: '30' }) return?
options: { ok: false, errors: { age: 'must be an integer from 13 to 120' } }
{ ok: false, errors: { email: 'must be an email' } }
cards.explain: Number.isInteger('30') is false because the value is a string, so age fails. The email is valid, so only age is reported.

cards.lessonTitle: Never trust input: validate at the edge
cards.prompt: A handler runs db.users.insert(req.body). A client posts { email, password, role: 'admin' }. What is the flaw?
options: JSON cannot contain a role field
Mass assignment: the client chose a field it should not control
cards.explain: The handler copies whatever the client sent. Build the record from explicitly named, validated fields so privileged fields can only be set by your own code.

cards.lessonTitle: Never trust input: validate at the edge
cards.prompt: A valid name O'Brien is concatenated into an SQL string and the query fails. Which fix addresses the actual problem?
options: Use a parameterised query so the value is never parsed as SQL
Convert the name to lower case
cards.explain: The name is legitimate input. The bug is building SQL from strings. Parameters keep data and code separate at the point of use, which validation alone cannot do.

cards.lessonTitle: Coercion, defaults and error responses
cards.prompt: What does Number('') evaluate to in JavaScript?
cards.explain: An empty or whitespace-only string converts to 0, which is why ?limit= can silently become a limit of zero if you convert without checking the text first.

cards.lessonTitle: Coercion, defaults and error responses
cards.prompt: What does parseInt('12abc') return?
cards.explain: parseInt reads digits from the start and stops at the first character that does not fit, so it returns 12. Number('12abc') would be NaN. The two behave differently.

cards.lessonTitle: Coercion, defaults and error responses
cards.prompt: A handler uses const limit = Number(req.query.limit) || 20. A client sends ?limit=0 to ask for no items. What happens?
options: limit is 20, because 0 is falsy and || replaces it
cards.explain: || treats 0 as 'missing'. Decide explicitly whether 0 is valid, and apply defaults only when the value is actually undefined.

cards.lessonTitle: Coercion, defaults and error responses
cards.prompt: A client sends a JSON body with an invalid field. Which response best helps them and keeps monitoring useful?
options: 500 Internal Server Error with a stack trace
400 with a stable error code and per-field messages
cards.explain: A 4xx status tells caches, proxies and monitoring that the client was wrong, and per-field details let the client fix the request without exposing server internals.

cards.lessonTitle: Layers: controllers, services and repositories
cards.prompt: The rule 'a transfer may not exceed the account balance' belongs in which layer?
cards.explain: It is a business rule. The service can then be tested with plain function calls and reused by any entry point, while the controller only translates HTTP.

cards.lessonTitle: Layers: controllers, services and repositories
cards.prompt: In the example, what status does postTransfer return when the sender's balance is too small?
cards.explain: The service throws InsufficientFunds, and the controller maps that domain error to 409 Conflict. 400 is for a malformed amount and 404 for an unknown account.

cards.lessonTitle: Layers: controllers, services and repositories
cards.prompt: A service function takes (req, res) and reads req.body directly. What problem does this create?
options: It cannot be reused from a queue worker or tested without faking HTTP
cards.explain: The service is now coupled to HTTP. Pass plain values in and return plain values or throw domain errors, and the controller handles the request and response.

cards.lessonTitle: Layers: controllers, services and repositories
cards.prompt: You are building three read-only endpoints that each run one query and return it. Which approach fits best?
options: Full controller, service and repository for each
A simple handler per route, adding layers when rules or reuse appear
Put all queries in the frontend
cards.explain: Layers earn their cost when there is logic to protect or reuse. Adding them to trivial reads is ceremony; refactor when the need appears.

cards.lessonTitle: Middleware: a pipeline around your handler
cards.prompt: With the chain timing > auth > handler and an anonymous request, which entries are logged?
cards.explain: auth short-circuits without calling next, so the handler never runs. timing still logs on the way out because its await next() returns once the chain stops.

cards.lessonTitle: Middleware: a pipeline around your handler
cards.prompt: A middleware checks a header, and for bad values it just returns without calling next() or sending anything. What does the client experience?
options: A hung request until it times out
cards.explain: Nothing answers the request and nothing continues the chain, so the connection stays open. Either call next() or send a response on every path.

cards.lessonTitle: Middleware: a pipeline around your handler
cards.prompt: Where should the authentication middleware sit relative to the route handlers it protects?
cards.explain: Middleware runs in order, so authentication must come first for its short-circuit to prevent the handler from running at all.

cards.lessonTitle: Middleware: a pipeline around your handler
cards.prompt: A middleware stores the current user in a module-level variable that handlers read. Under concurrent requests, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing, Node runs one request at a time
One request can read another request's user
cards.explain: Requests interleave at every await. A shared variable is overwritten by whichever request wrote last, so use the request object or async-local storage for per-request data.

cards.lessonTitle: REST in practice: resources, status codes and idempotency
cards.prompt: Which method is NOT guaranteed to be idempotent?
cards.explain: Repeating a POST typically creates another resource or repeats the side effect. PUT, DELETE and GET are defined so that repeating them leaves the same state.

cards.lessonTitle: REST in practice: resources, status codes and idempotency
cards.prompt: A POST successfully creates a new order. Which response is most appropriate?
cards.explain: 201 says a resource was created, and Location tells the client where to find it. 202 is for work accepted but not yet done.

cards.lessonTitle: REST in practice: resources, status codes and idempotency
cards.prompt: A mobile client times out waiting for POST /payments and retries. How do you prevent a double charge?
options: Require an Idempotency-Key and return the stored result on repeats
cards.explain: The key lets the server recognise the repeat of one intended operation and answer with the first result instead of charging again.

cards.lessonTitle: REST in practice: resources, status codes and idempotency
cards.prompt: A site deletes accounts through GET /users/42/delete, and a search-engine crawler deletes users. What was violated?
options: GET is supposed to be safe, so it must not change state
cards.explain: Crawlers, prefetchers and caches assume GET has no side effects. State changes belong on POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.

cards.lessonTitle: Pagination, filtering and versioning
cards.prompt: Rows 1 to 10 exist. A client reads page 1 (offset 0, limit 3 = rows 1,2,3). Row 2 is then deleted. What does offset 3, limit 3 return?
cards.explain: After the delete, rows shift down by one, so offset 3 starts at row 5. Row 4 moved into the already-read window and is never returned. A cursor 'after id 3' would return 4, 5, 6.

cards.lessonTitle: Pagination, filtering and versioning
cards.prompt: Why does keyset pagination stay fast on deep pages?
options: An index lets the database jump directly to the last-seen key instead of counting past skipped rows
cards.explain: WHERE id > :last uses the index to seek to a position. OFFSET has to step over every skipped row each time.

cards.lessonTitle: Pagination, filtering and versioning
cards.prompt: An endpoint builds SQL as 'ORDER BY ' + req.query.sort. What is the problem?
options: The client controls part of the SQL, which allows injection
cards.explain: Column names cannot be parameterised, so map the requested sort onto a fixed allow-list of known columns instead of concatenating client text.

cards.lessonTitle: Pagination, filtering and versioning
cards.prompt: Which change to GET /users/42 most likely breaks existing clients?
options: Renaming the field name to fullName
cards.explain: A client reading user.name now gets undefined. Additions are usually safe; renames and removals break correct clients and need a new version or a transition period.

cards.lessonTitle: Inside a database: pages, the write-ahead log and row versions
cards.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what is the basic unit the database reads from and writes to storage for table data?
cards.explain: Storage is handled in fixed-size pages. Reading one row means loading its whole page, which is why page counts determine scan cost.

cards.lessonTitle: Inside a database: pages, the write-ahead log and row versions
cards.prompt: Why is the log written before the data page is changed on disk?
options: Logs are smaller, so it saves space
So committed changes can be replayed after a crash even if the data page never reached disk
Because pages cannot be written at all
cards.explain: Write-ahead means the description of the change is durable first. Recovery replays it, so a commit that returned can never be lost to a crash.

cards.lessonTitle: Inside a database: pages, the write-ahead log and row versions
cards.prompt: A row has ctid (0,1). After UPDATE ... WHERE id = 1, you select its ctid again. What is most likely?
options: A different value, because UPDATE wrote a new row version
cards.explain: PostgreSQL writes a new tuple for each update, so the visible row now has a different ctid. The old version is dead until vacuum reclaims it.

cards.lessonTitle: Inside a database: pages, the write-ahead log and row versions
cards.prompt: A table that is updated heavily gets slower over weeks although its live row count is constant. What is a likely cause?
options: Dead row versions accumulate faster than vacuum removes them, so scans read more pages
cards.explain: Each update leaves a dead version behind. Without enough vacuuming the table bloats, so the same number of live rows now spans many more pages.

cards.lessonTitle: Connections and connection pools
cards.prompt: What is the main reason to use a connection pool?
options: It avoids the cost of opening a connection per request and bounds concurrent load on the database
It makes queries return more rows
cards.explain: Connections are expensive to create and limited in number. A pool reuses a bounded set and queues the excess instead of overwhelming the server.

cards.lessonTitle: Connections and connection pools
cards.prompt: A pool has max 2 connections. Six queries, each taking 100 ms, are started at the same time. Roughly when does the last one finish?
cards.explain: Two run at a time, so the six queries complete in three waves of 100 ms each. The pool bounded the concurrency to two.

cards.lessonTitle: Connections and connection pools
cards.prompt: After some hours every request hangs waiting for a connection, although the database is idle. What is the likely bug?
options: The database ran out of disk
Connections are borrowed and never released on some code path
The pool size is too big
cards.explain: Leaked connections stay marked in use, so the pool slowly runs out and later requests wait forever. Release in a finally block and set an acquire timeout.

cards.lessonTitle: Connections and connection pools
cards.prompt: Your database allows 100 connections. You plan 20 app instances, each with a pool of 10. What is the problem?
options: Together they can open 200 connections, above the limit
Pools only work with one instance
The instances will share one pool automatically
cards.explain: Total possible connections is instances times pool size. Reduce the per-instance pool or use an external pooler that multiplexes them.

cards.lessonTitle: gRPC and Protocol Buffers: typed service-to-service calls
cards.prompt: What identifies a field in a protobuf message on the wire?
cards.explain: Messages carry field numbers and values; names exist only in the schema.

cards.lessonTitle: gRPC and Protocol Buffers: typed service-to-service calls
cards.prompt: In a varint, 150 is encoded as 96 01. Why does it take two bytes?
options: Each byte holds 7 bits and 150 needs more than 7 bits, so a continuation bit is set
cards.explain: Values up to 127 fit in one byte. 150 exceeds that, so the first byte carries the low 7 bits with the high bit set, and the next byte carries the rest.

cards.lessonTitle: gRPC and Protocol Buffers: typed service-to-service calls
cards.prompt: A team deletes field 3 and later adds a new field also numbered 3 with a different type. Old data in a queue is now garbled. What went wrong?
options: A field number was reused, so old bytes are decoded as the new field
cards.explain: Field numbers are permanent identities. Reserve removed numbers and never reuse them.

cards.lessonTitle: gRPC and Protocol Buffers: typed service-to-service calls
cards.prompt: You expose a public API to third-party developers using browsers and curl. Which is the safer default?
options: REST over HTTP with JSON, possibly with gRPC inside your network
cards.explain: Public APIs favour universality and easy debugging. gRPC shines between services you control.

cards.lessonTitle: Configuration, environments and secrets
cards.prompt: Why validate configuration at startup?
options: A bad value fails immediately with a clear message instead of causing a hard-to-trace error later
It removes the need for tests
cards.explain: Failing fast at boot turns a latent production surprise into an obvious deploy-time error.

cards.lessonTitle: Configuration, environments and secrets
cards.prompt: An API key was pushed to GitHub and removed in the next commit. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as compromised: revoke and rotate it, then review usage
cards.explain: History and forks retain the secret, and automated scanners find them quickly. Rotation is the fix.

cards.lessonTitle: Configuration, environments and secrets
cards.prompt: PORT=4000 is set in the environment. What type does process.env.PORT have in Node?
cards.explain: Environment variables are always strings. Parse and validate them into the types you need.

cards.lessonTitle: Configuration, environments and secrets
cards.prompt: A staging key was reused in production 'to save time', and a staging leak exposed production data. What principle was broken?
options: Separation of secrets per environment and least privilege
cards.explain: Each environment should have its own credentials with the minimum rights, so a leak has a limited blast radius.

cards.lessonTitle: Tables, keys, constraints and joins
cards.prompt: customers has Asha, Ben and Chen. Chen has no orders. What does customers LEFT JOIN orders return for Chen?
options: One row for Chen with NULL order columns
cards.explain: A left join keeps every left-side row; when nothing matches, the right-side columns are NULL. An inner join would drop Chen.

cards.lessonTitle: Tables, keys, constraints and joins
cards.prompt: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) returns no rows, yet Chen has no orders. Why?
options: Chen is hidden by a bug in PostgreSQL
orders.customer_id contains a NULL, which makes NOT IN never true
NOT IN is not valid SQL
cards.explain: With a NULL in the list, 'id <> NULL' is unknown, so no row can satisfy NOT IN. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out.

cards.lessonTitle: Tables, keys, constraints and joins
cards.prompt: A table has 4 rows and 1 of them has a NULL in column x. What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(x) return?
cards.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.

cards.lessonTitle: Tables, keys, constraints and joins
cards.prompt: Three services and a nightly script all write to the orders table. Where should the rule 'total must not be negative' be enforced?
options: In the database with a CHECK constraint, plus application validation for good error messages
cards.explain: Only the database sees every write. A constraint guarantees the rule for all writers, and application validation gives users a friendlier message before the constraint is hit.

cards.lessonTitle: Normalisation and safe schema migrations
cards.prompt: A customer's city is stored in every one of their order rows, and you update only some of them. What is this called?
cards.explain: Repeated data means one fact must be changed in many places. Missing one leaves contradictory values, which is an update anomaly.

cards.lessonTitle: Normalisation and safe schema migrations
cards.prompt: Migration 0003 already ran in staging and production, and you notice a typo in it. What should you do?
options: Add a new migration 0004 that corrects it
cards.explain: Environments that already applied 0003 will never rerun it, so editing it makes them differ. A new migration moves everyone forward the same way.

cards.lessonTitle: Normalisation and safe schema migrations
cards.prompt: You rename a column in one migration and deploy new code in the same release. During the rolling deploy, old app instances still run. What happens?
options: Old instances query the missing column and fail until they are replaced
The database restores the old name
cards.explain: Old and new versions overlap during a rollout, so a schema change must work for both. That is why renames use expand and contract.

cards.lessonTitle: Normalisation and safe schema migrations
cards.prompt: A team backfills 50 million rows with one UPDATE statement in a single transaction and the site slows to a crawl. What is the better approach?
options: Backfill in small batches, committing between them
cards.explain: A giant transaction holds locks, creates many dead row versions and a huge log. Small batches keep each transaction short and the system responsive.

cards.lessonTitle: B-tree indexes: from a full scan to a handful of page reads
cards.prompt: Why is a B-tree lookup on a million rows only a few page reads?
options: The table is cached in the browser
Each node is a page with hundreds of keys, so the tree is very shallow
It stores the answer in the WAL
cards.explain: High fan-out means few levels. Each level costs one page read, so the cost is logarithmic with a large base.

cards.lessonTitle: B-tree indexes: from a full scan to a handful of page reads
cards.prompt: There is a B-tree index on email. Which query can use it efficiently?
cards.explain: Equality lets the index seek directly. A leading wildcard, a function on the column or a negation does not give a sorted range to seek to.

cards.lessonTitle: B-tree indexes: from a full scan to a handful of page reads
cards.prompt: A query filters on country = 'IN' and 20 percent of all rows match. What is likely to happen even if country is indexed?
options: The planner reads a large share of the table anyway, so the index barely helps
cards.explain: Returning a big fraction of rows means visiting most pages regardless. Indexes shine when they let you skip most of the data.

cards.lessonTitle: B-tree indexes: from a full scan to a handful of page reads
cards.prompt: You have an index on (country, created_at). Which filter alone benefits most?
cards.explain: A composite index is sorted by its leftmost column first. Filtering on country alone can seek into it; created_at alone cannot.

cards.lessonTitle: Reading EXPLAIN: how to see what the database actually does
cards.prompt: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
options: EXPLAIN shows an estimated plan; ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real timings
cards.explain: Plain EXPLAIN never executes the statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE does, so it reports actual time and row counts.

cards.lessonTitle: Reading EXPLAIN: how to see what the database actually does
cards.prompt: A plan shows Seq Scan with 'Rows Removed by Filter: 1000000' and rows=1. What does it suggest?
options: An index on the filtered column would likely help
cards.explain: Scanning a million rows to keep one is exactly what a selective index avoids.

cards.lessonTitle: Reading EXPLAIN: how to see what the database actually does
cards.prompt: You want the real timing of a slow DELETE on production. What is the safe way?
options: Wrap it in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, or test on a copy
cards.explain: ANALYZE executes the statement, so the rows would really be deleted. A rolled-back transaction or a copy keeps the data safe.

cards.lessonTitle: Reading EXPLAIN: how to see what the database actually does
cards.prompt: The plan estimates 10 rows but actually returns 800 000. What is the most likely cause?
options: Stale or misleading statistics, so the planner chose a plan for the wrong size
The query has a syntax error
cards.explain: Large estimate errors mean the planner reasoned from wrong numbers. Refresh statistics with ANALYZE and re-check the plan.

cards.lessonTitle: Transactions and ACID
cards.prompt: A transfer subtracts from account A, then the server crashes before adding to account B. With a transaction, what is the state after recovery?
cards.explain: The transaction never committed, so none of its changes become visible. That is atomicity.

cards.lessonTitle: Transactions and ACID
cards.prompt: Which mechanism lets a committed transaction survive a crash?
options: The write-ahead log flushed at commit
cards.explain: Commit returns after the log record is durable. Recovery replays it, so the change is not lost.

cards.lessonTitle: Transactions and ACID
cards.prompt: Code runs await pool.query('BEGIN'), then two updates with pool.query, then pool.query('COMMIT'). Rollback never restores anything. Why?
options: Each call may use a different connection, so the statements are not in one transaction
cards.explain: A transaction lives on one session. You must check out a single client and run every statement on it.

cards.lessonTitle: Transactions and ACID
cards.prompt: Inside a transaction you call a payment API, then update the order. The API takes 3 seconds. What goes wrong at scale?
options: Locks and a connection are held for seconds, and if the transaction fails after the charge you cannot roll the charge back
cards.explain: Slow external calls inside a transaction hold resources and cannot be rolled back. Commit first and perform the side effect afterwards, ideally with an outbox.

cards.lessonTitle: Isolation levels, anomalies and lost updates
cards.prompt: Which isolation level does PostgreSQL use by default?
cards.explain: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed. Each statement sees data committed before that statement started.

cards.lessonTitle: Isolation levels, anomalies and lost updates
cards.prompt: Two requests each read balance 100, add 10 in application code and write back, at read committed. What is the final balance?
cards.explain: Both computed 110 from the same old value, so the second write overwrote the first. An atomic UPDATE bal = bal + 10 gives 120.

cards.lessonTitle: Isolation levels, anomalies and lost updates
cards.prompt: At least one doctor must stay on call. Two doctors each check the count, see two, and go off call at the same time. Which technique reliably prevents zero on call?
options: Serializable isolation with retry, or locking the rows that were read
cards.explain: The transactions write different rows, so ordinary row locks do not conflict. Serializable detects the dependency; locking the read set also works.

cards.lessonTitle: Isolation levels, anomalies and lost updates
cards.prompt: A serializable transaction fails with a serialization error. The code retries only the last UPDATE. What is wrong?
options: The transaction was aborted; the whole transaction, including its reads, must be rerun from BEGIN
It should switch to read committed
cards.explain: The decision depended on earlier reads that may now be stale. Rerun the whole unit of work on a fresh snapshot.

cards.lessonTitle: NoSQL and data-model trade-offs
cards.prompt: Which store type is built for fast lookup by a single key, such as a session id?
cards.explain: Key-value stores are optimised for get and set by key, with almost no query capability beyond that.

cards.lessonTitle: NoSQL and data-model trade-offs
cards.prompt: A jsonb column has a GIN index and you query for rows containing type buy with the containment operator. Compared with no index on 300 000 rows, what is likely?
options: Orders of magnitude faster because the index finds matches without scanning every row
cards.explain: A GIN index on jsonb supports containment queries, avoiding a sequential scan. In the lab it went from about 51 ms to under 1 ms.

cards.lessonTitle: NoSQL and data-model trade-offs
cards.prompt: A report that sums the user field fails because one document stores user as the string 'forty-two'. What is the underlying cause?
options: No database-enforced types, so a bad shape was accepted at write time
cards.explain: Schema flexibility moves validation into your code. Validate on write and version documents.

cards.lessonTitle: NoSQL and data-model trade-offs
cards.prompt: You need orders with transactions and joins to customers, plus a flexible bag of per-product attributes. What is a sound starting design?
options: Relational tables with a jsonb column for the flexible attributes
cards.explain: Keep transactional, relational data in tables and put only the variable part in jsonb, with one database and one backup story.

cards.lessonTitle: Caching with Redis: cache-aside, TTLs and eviction
cards.prompt: In cache-aside, what does the application do on a cache miss?
options: Reads the database, stores the result in the cache, then returns it
Waits for the cache to fill itself
cards.explain: The application loads from the source of truth and populates the cache so the next request can hit.

cards.lessonTitle: Caching with Redis: cache-aside, TTLs and eviction
cards.prompt: Traffic is uniform over 10 000 keys and the cache holds 1 000. Roughly what hit rate should you expect?
cards.explain: With uniform access each request has a 1 000 in 10 000 chance of asking for a cached key. Caches pay off when traffic is skewed.

cards.lessonTitle: Caching with Redis: cache-aside, TTLs and eviction
cards.prompt: After a traffic spike, SET commands fail with 'OOM command not allowed'. What is the likely configuration?
options: maxmemory-policy is noeviction and memory is full
The key names are too short
cards.explain: With noeviction Redis rejects writes once memory is full. Use an evicting policy if it is a cache, or add memory and alerts if it is a store.

cards.lessonTitle: Caching with Redis: cache-aside, TTLs and eviction
cards.prompt: Prices change a few times a day, and showing a price up to five minutes old is acceptable. How should you set the cache?
options: A TTL of about five minutes, plus deleting the key on price changes
cards.explain: A TTL expresses the staleness budget and caps the damage of a missed invalidation; deleting on write makes updates visible sooner.

cards.lessonTitle: Cache invalidation and stampedes
cards.prompt: A hot key expires and 100 requests arrive at once; each miss queries the database. Without protection, how many database queries run?
cards.explain: Every request misses and none knows the others are loading the same value, so all 100 query the database.

cards.lessonTitle: Cache invalidation and stampedes
cards.prompt: What does single-flight do?
options: Limits the cache to one key
Lets the first miss load the value while other requests wait for that same result
cards.explain: Concurrent requests for the same missing key share one in-flight load, so the database sees one query.

cards.lessonTitle: Cache invalidation and stampedes
cards.prompt: Right after a profile update the old name appears for ten minutes, though you delete the cache key on every write. What is the likely cause?
options: A reader cached the old row just after your delete, so the stale value stays until its TTL
cards.explain: A read that began before the write can store its old result after the delete. A TTL bounds how long that stale copy survives.

cards.lessonTitle: Cache invalidation and stampedes
cards.prompt: Ten thousand keys are all cached for exactly 60 seconds when the service starts. What happens a minute later?
options: They expire together and a wave of misses hits the database
cards.explain: Synchronised expiry causes a burst of misses. Random jitter on the TTL spreads them out.

cards.lessonTitle: Task queues and workers
cards.prompt: Why send an email from a background worker instead of inside the HTTP request?
options: The request returns fast and a slow or failing email service cannot break it
cards.explain: Moving slow, failure-prone work out of the request keeps latency low and lets you retry independently.

cards.lessonTitle: Task queues and workers
cards.prompt: Two workers run the claim query at once with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. What happens?
options: Each gets different jobs and neither waits
The second waits for the first to commit
cards.explain: SKIP LOCKED skips rows the other worker has locked, so claims do not overlap and do not block.

cards.lessonTitle: Task queues and workers
cards.prompt: A worker sends an email, then crashes before marking the job done. What will happen, and what does it imply?
options: The job is retried and the email may be sent twice, so jobs must tolerate duplicates
cards.explain: At-least-once delivery means a finished-but-unacknowledged job runs again. Design the job to be idempotent.

cards.lessonTitle: Task queues and workers
cards.prompt: Users sometimes get an order saved but no confirmation email is ever sent. The code commits the order, then enqueues the job. Why?
options: The process can die between the commit and the enqueue, losing the job
Orders and jobs share a primary key
cards.explain: Two separate steps can be split by a crash. Insert the job in the same transaction as the order (outbox) so both happen or neither.

cards.lessonTitle: Retries, backoff and idempotent jobs
cards.prompt: Base delay 100 ms, factor 2, no cap. How long is the wait before the 5th retry?
cards.explain: The waits double: 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. The fifth wait is 1600 ms.

cards.lessonTitle: Retries, backoff and idempotent jobs
cards.prompt: Why add jitter to backoff?
options: So clients do not all retry at the same instant
cards.explain: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together. Randomising spreads the load.

cards.lessonTitle: Retries, backoff and idempotent jobs
cards.prompt: A job adds 10 to a user's points. It is retried after a crash. How do you prevent double-crediting?
options: Record the event id in a unique table in the same transaction and skip if it already exists
cards.explain: A unique processed-event record turns the repeated delivery into a no-op, and committing it with the credit keeps both atomic.

cards.lessonTitle: Retries, backoff and idempotent jobs
cards.prompt: A brief database blip causes a huge spike of 27 requests per original call. Client, gateway and worker each retry 3 times. What is the fix?
options: Choose one layer to retry and have the others fail fast
cards.explain: Retries at every layer multiply (3 x 3 x 3). Retry at one place with backoff, jitter and a cap.

cards.lessonTitle: Full-text search: inverted indexes, stemming and ranking
cards.prompt: Why is a full-text search for a rare word fast with an inverted index?
options: It looks the word up and reads only the listed documents
cards.explain: The index maps each word to the documents containing it, so only matching documents are visited.

cards.lessonTitle: Full-text search: inverted indexes, stemming and ranking
cards.prompt: to_tsvector('english', 'The caches were running quickly') is matched with to_tsquery('english', 'run & cache'). What is the result?
options: true, stemming reduces both sides to the same tokens
cards.explain: Stemming turns caches into cach and running into run, and the query is normalised the same way, so they match.

cards.lessonTitle: Full-text search: inverted indexes, stemming and ranking
cards.prompt: You created a GIN index on to_tsvector('english', body) but queries using to_tsvector('simple', body) are slow. Why?
options: The query expression differs from the indexed one, so the index cannot be used
cards.explain: An expression index only serves queries that use the identical expression and configuration.

cards.lessonTitle: Full-text search: inverted indexes, stemming and ranking
cards.prompt: You need typo tolerance, faceted filters and tuned relevance across 50 million documents. What is the usual choice?
options: A dedicated search engine kept in sync with the source of truth
cards.explain: Search engines specialise in relevance, typo tolerance and scale. Keep the primary database authoritative and feed the engine from it.

cards.lessonTitle: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth
cards.prompt: After a deploy, some new products never appear in search. The handler saves to the database and then calls the search engine. What is the likely cause?
options: A failure or crash between the two writes left the index without the record (dual-write problem)
cards.explain: Two separate writes cannot be atomic. An outbox row inserted in the same transaction makes the intent durable and retryable.

cards.lessonTitle: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth
cards.prompt: What is the key property of the transactional outbox?
options: It makes the search engine faster
The change and the instruction to index it commit in one database transaction
cards.explain: Because both rows commit together, a worker can always find and retry the pending index operation.

cards.lessonTitle: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth
cards.prompt: A user's access to a private document is revoked, but it still appears in their search results for a minute. How should authorization be handled?
options: Check permissions against the source of truth when returning results, not only in the index
cards.explain: The index lags. Enforce access on the authoritative records or with promptly updated permission data.

cards.lessonTitle: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth
cards.prompt: You rebuild the search index in place while users search. What may they see?
options: Missing or partial results during the rebuild
cards.explain: In-place rebuilds expose a half-built index. Build a new index and switch an alias when it is complete.

cards.lessonTitle: Timeouts, circuit breakers and failing fast
cards.prompt: Why is a slow dependency often worse than a dead one?
options: Callers wait on it, holding resources until their own service is exhausted
cards.explain: A refused connection fails immediately, while a hang holds your threads and connections until something gives.

cards.lessonTitle: Timeouts, circuit breakers and failing fast
cards.prompt: A circuit breaker is open. A request arrives. What happens?
options: It is sent to the dependency
It is rejected immediately without calling the dependency
cards.explain: Open means fail fast. After the cool-down a few trial calls test whether the dependency recovered.

cards.lessonTitle: Timeouts, circuit breakers and failing fast
cards.prompt: Your endpoint must answer within 1 second and calls two services in sequence. What should their timeouts roughly add up to?
options: Together comfortably less than 1 second, leaving room for your own work
cards.explain: Timeouts are a budget. The total of the chain must fit within what you promised your own caller.

cards.lessonTitle: Timeouts, circuit breakers and failing fast
cards.prompt: During a partner outage your service runs out of threads and stops answering health checks. The HTTP client has default settings. What is the likely problem?
options: No outbound timeout, so requests hang and accumulate
cards.explain: Default clients often wait indefinitely. Always set explicit timeouts on outbound calls.

cards.lessonTitle: Retry storms, overload and cascading failure
cards.prompt: Capacity is 100 rps. Clients send 100 rps and retry each failure 3 times immediately during an outage. What load hits the service?
cards.explain: Each original request plus three retries makes four attempts, so 100 times 4 is 400 rps against a capacity of 100.

cards.lessonTitle: Retry storms, overload and cascading failure
cards.prompt: Why can a long queue make an overloaded service useless?
options: Requests wait longer than clients will, so the server finishes work nobody is waiting for
cards.explain: Once wait time exceeds the client timeout, the server spends capacity on answers that are discarded, so useful throughput collapses.

cards.lessonTitle: Retry storms, overload and cascading failure
cards.prompt: A service is saturated and every request is slow. What is a better strategy than letting all requests wait?
options: Reject a share of requests quickly so the rest finish within their deadlines
cards.explain: Shedding load keeps latency bounded for accepted requests. Failing some fast beats failing all slowly.

cards.lessonTitle: Retry storms, overload and cascading failure
cards.prompt: The database fault was fixed 10 minutes ago, but the API still times out and CPU stays at 100 percent. What is the likely mechanism?
options: A backlog and retries keep the service above capacity even without the original fault
cards.explain: Overload can be self-sustaining. Shed load or cut traffic to let the system drain before restoring it gradually.

cards.lessonTitle: Logs, metrics and traces
cards.prompt: Out of 10 000 requests, 2 percent take about one second and the rest about 30 ms. Which statistic best reveals the problem?
cards.explain: The mean and median look healthy. The 99th percentile falls inside the slow 2 percent and exposes the tail.

cards.lessonTitle: Logs, metrics and traces
cards.prompt: A user reports an error at 21:14. Which single piece of data lets you find every log line across services for that request?
options: A request id carried through all services
cards.explain: A request id attached to each log line and forwarded downstream joins the whole request's activity.

cards.lessonTitle: Logs, metrics and traces
cards.prompt: Which signal best shows which downstream call consumed most of a request's 400 ms?
cards.explain: A trace breaks one request into timed spans across services, showing where the time went.

cards.lessonTitle: Logs, metrics and traces
cards.prompt: After adding a user_id label to a request counter, the metrics system slows and its bill triples. Why?
options: Each distinct user creates its own time series (high cardinality)
The label name is too long
cards.explain: Every unique label value is a separate series. Keep labels to small sets such as route and status.

cards.lessonTitle: SLOs, alerts and a method for debugging production
cards.prompt: An SLO is 99.5 percent over 28 days. Roughly how much total downtime does the error budget allow?
cards.explain: 28 days is 672 hours, and 0.5 percent of that is about 3.4 hours.

cards.lessonTitle: SLOs, alerts and a method for debugging production
cards.prompt: Which alert is best to page a human at night?
options: CPU above 80 percent for one minute
Error rate far above the SLO budget burn rate, affecting users
cards.explain: Page on user-visible symptoms and fast budget burn, not on causes that may be harmless.

cards.lessonTitle: SLOs, alerts and a method for debugging production
cards.prompt: Errors spike five minutes after a deploy. What is the right first move?
options: Roll back or disable the change to restore service, then investigate
cards.explain: Mitigate first. Rolling back is the fastest safe action when the change is the likely cause.

cards.lessonTitle: SLOs, alerts and a method for debugging production
cards.prompt: What does 'blameless' mean in a postmortem?
options: Focus on the system and process conditions that allowed the failure, not on punishing a person
cards.explain: Blameless reviews ask what allowed the incident, which finds fixable causes and keeps people honest about what happened.

cards.lessonTitle: Graceful shutdown: stopping without dropping requests
cards.prompt: Which order is right for a graceful shutdown?
options: Close the database pool, then stop accepting requests
Stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, close resources, exit
cards.explain: Closing resources first would break requests still being served. Drain, then close, then exit.

cards.lessonTitle: Graceful shutdown: stopping without dropping requests
cards.prompt: After SIGTERM your server's close() callback never fires although no requests are active. What is a likely cause?
options: Idle keep-alive connections are still open and keep the server alive
Node is too old to exit
cards.explain: Idle keep-alive sockets keep the server from finishing close(). Close idle connections explicitly and enforce a deadline.

cards.lessonTitle: Graceful shutdown: stopping without dropping requests
cards.prompt: Right after a deploy starts, a few users get connection errors although the app handles SIGTERM. What is likely happening?
options: The load balancer still sent requests to the instance after it stopped accepting connections
cards.explain: Removal from the balancer and the stop signal race each other. Fail readiness first and pause briefly before closing the listener.

cards.lessonTitle: Graceful shutdown: stopping without dropping requests
cards.prompt: What should a background worker do on SIGTERM?
options: Claim as many jobs as possible
Stop claiming new jobs, finish or release the current one, then exit
cards.explain: Stop taking new work and leave the queue consistent. An unfinished claim returns to the queue and another worker takes it.

cards.lessonTitle: Injection, password storage and where trust ends
cards.prompt: What actually prevents SQL injection?
options: Parameterised queries that send values separately from the SQL
cards.explain: With parameters the database never parses the value as SQL, whatever characters it holds.

cards.lessonTitle: Injection, password storage and where trust ends
cards.prompt: Roughly how much slower is one scrypt (N=16384) guess than one SHA-256 guess, on the same CPU?
cards.explain: In the measurement, about 38 ms versus 0.0025 ms per hash, a factor of roughly 15 000 to 20 000. That is the point of a slow hash.

cards.lessonTitle: Injection, password storage and where trust ends
cards.prompt: A checkout request body contains a list of items and a total field set to 1. Where should the server get the total from?
options: From the request, it is already computed
Recompute it on the server from trusted prices
cards.explain: Anything the client sends can be forged. Authoritative values such as prices are looked up and computed server-side.

cards.lessonTitle: Injection, password storage and where trust ends
cards.prompt: An SQL injection bug is found. The app connects to the database as a superuser. Why does that make the incident worse?
options: The attacker inherits superuser rights and can read or destroy everything
cards.explain: A compromised query runs with the connection's privileges. Least privilege limits what an injection can reach.

cards.lessonTitle: Rate limiting, abuse and the OWASP Top 10
cards.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 5 tokens per second. It starts full and 100 requests arrive within one second. About how many pass?
cards.explain: Ten tokens are available at once and about four more refill during that second, so roughly 14 pass and the rest get 429.

cards.lessonTitle: Rate limiting, abuse and the OWASP Top 10
cards.prompt: Your login limit is 5 attempts per minute, kept in each API instance's memory, and you run 4 instances. What can an attacker actually do?
options: About 20 attempts per minute, and a restart resets the counts
cards.explain: Each instance counts separately, so the effective limit multiplies with the instance count. A shared store gives one global count.

cards.lessonTitle: Rate limiting, abuse and the OWASP Top 10
cards.prompt: Changing /api/orders/17 to /api/orders/18 in the URL shows another user's order. Which category is this?
cards.explain: The server did not check that the order belongs to the caller. It is the most common category in the Top 10.

cards.lessonTitle: Rate limiting, abuse and the OWASP Top 10
cards.prompt: Login returns 'no such user' for unknown emails and 'wrong password' for known ones. What is the problem?
options: It reveals which emails are registered, enabling enumeration
cards.explain: Different messages let attackers discover valid accounts. Return one generic message and keep timing similar.

cards.lessonTitle: Reverse proxies and load balancing
cards.prompt: Requests vary from 10 ms to 400 ms. Round robin gives each server the same number of requests, yet one server's queue keeps growing. Why?
options: Equal request counts are not equal work, and round robin ignores current load
Round robin only works with two servers
cards.explain: A server that gets several slow requests falls behind while others idle. Least connections or power-of-two choices adapt to load.

cards.lessonTitle: Reverse proxies and load balancing
cards.prompt: A health check calls the database. The database has a 10-second hiccup and the whole site returns 503 even though the web servers are fine. Why?
options: All servers failed their check and were removed together
cards.explain: A dependency-heavy health check lets one shared failure remove every healthy server. Keep liveness checks local and cheap.

cards.lessonTitle: Reverse proxies and load balancing
cards.prompt: What is the main problem with sticky sessions used to keep in-memory login sessions?
options: Load becomes uneven and sessions are lost when that server dies or is redeployed
cards.explain: Pinning clients to servers hides state that should live in a shared store or a token.

cards.lessonTitle: Reverse proxies and load balancing
cards.prompt: You double the web servers behind a load balancer but latency does not improve; the database CPU is at 100 percent. What is the bottleneck?
cards.explain: More stateless servers cannot help if every request waits on one saturated database. Scale or relieve that component.

cards.lessonTitle: Replication, sharding and the limits of scaling
cards.prompt: A user updates their profile and immediately reloads, but sees the old data. Reads go to an asynchronous replica. What is happening?
options: The replica has not yet applied the change (replication lag)
cards.explain: Asynchronous replicas can be behind. Read your own writes from the primary for a short time.

cards.lessonTitle: Replication, sharding and the limits of scaling
cards.prompt: You grow a cache cluster from 4 to 5 nodes using hash(key) mod N. About what fraction of keys changes node?
cards.explain: Changing N remaps most keys under modulo hashing, around 80 percent here. Consistent hashing moves only about one fifth.

cards.lessonTitle: Replication, sharding and the limits of scaling
cards.prompt: Only 50 percent of a job can run in parallel. What is the best possible speedup, even with unlimited machines?
cards.explain: The serial half always remains, so the limit is 1 / (1 - 0.5) = 2.

cards.lessonTitle: Replication, sharding and the limits of scaling
cards.prompt: Which should usually come before sharding a slow database?
options: Fix slow queries and indexes, add caching and read replicas, and scale vertically
Switch to a bigger load balancer
cards.explain: Sharding is complex and hard to undo. Exhaust cheaper options and measure that one machine truly cannot cope.

cards.lessonTitle: Race conditions, locks and atomic operations
cards.prompt: bal is 100. Two calls each run: read bal, await 10 ms, write read+10. Both start together. What is bal afterwards?
cards.explain: Both read 100 before either wrote, so both write 110. The await opened the race window even on one thread.

cards.lessonTitle: Race conditions, locks and atomic operations
cards.prompt: Why does Atomics.add avoid lost updates?
options: It runs on a faster thread
The read-modify-write happens as one indivisible operation
cards.explain: Atomic operations cannot be interleaved by other threads, so each increment sees the previous result.

cards.lessonTitle: Race conditions, locks and atomic operations
cards.prompt: Two signup requests with the same email both succeed, creating duplicates. The code checks 'does the email exist' and then inserts. What is the robust fix?
options: A unique constraint on email so the database enforces it atomically
cards.explain: Check-then-act is racy. A unique constraint makes the check and the insert one atomic decision in the database.

cards.lessonTitle: Race conditions, locks and atomic operations
cards.prompt: You protect a counter with an in-memory mutex and then run four server instances. What happens?
options: Each instance has its own mutex, so the instances can still race on shared data
cards.explain: An in-process lock protects only that process. Cross-instance state needs the database or another shared coordinator.

cards.lessonTitle: Deadlocks, scheduling and worker models
cards.prompt: T1 holds lock A and waits for B. T2 holds B and waits for A. Nothing errors and the service stops responding for those tasks. What is this?
options: A deadlock caused by circular wait
cards.explain: Each task waits for a lock the other holds, so neither can proceed. There is no error because nothing is failing, only waiting.

cards.lessonTitle: Deadlocks, scheduling and worker models
